name: i-Ready
line: i-Ready tests three times a year and assigns lessons. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs i-Ready: i-Ready tests three times a year and assigns lessons. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: i-Ready tests a student in fall, winter and spring and assigns a path of lessons from the result [8][10]. In AMP, assessment is continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem. Each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer, and learned skills keep returning in practice.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no test day. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. i-Ready sets a path of lessons from a diagnostic given in fall, winter and spring, and teachers can add lessons or change the order [8][10].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In i-Ready the unit is the lesson: instruction, then practice, then a scored quiz at the end [9].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. Seventh graders in a WestEd study of i-Ready wanted to know exactly which answers they got wrong [5]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest effect [12].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once, and moves on. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In i-Ready a failed lesson is assigned again, and after a second failure the company's guide for educators turns to the teacher [9]. Students in the WestEd study asked for a way to test out of lessons on what they already knew [5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. We found no scheduled review of earlier skills in the i-Ready pages and guide we read [1][8][9][10]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [11].

reasons.title: Regular practice, not a supplement
reasons.body: AMP is built for regular use, as a learner's main math practice. Curriculum Associates describes i-Ready's lessons as a supplement to classroom instruction [1]. In the strongest independent study, math users averaged about twenty lessons in a school year, and the authors write that online tools appear most effective at 40 to 100 hours a school year [2].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math and runs from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. i-Ready Personalized Instruction covers kindergarten through grade 8 [1].

rows.start: A separate adaptive test, given in fall, winter and spring [8].
rows.teaching: Online lessons that combine instruction with practice and end in a scored quiz [9].
rows.next: A path of lessons built from the test. Teachers can add lessons or change the order [10].
rows.mastery: Passing the quiz at the end of a lesson. A failed lesson is assigned again [9].
rows.review: No scheduled review of earlier skills found in the pages and guide we read [1][8][9][10].
rows.adult: A teacher sets time, watches pass rates, assigns lessons and helps students who fail them [9].
rows.reports: Scores, placement levels and national percentiles from the test [13]. Time and pass rates from lessons [9].
rows.evidence: Strongest independent study: users 0.04 to 0.05 SD higher in math, described as not causal [2].

theirs: i-Ready comes from Curriculum Associates and is one of the most widely used programs in American schools [7]. This page is about its adaptive diagnostic and i-Ready Personalized Instruction for Mathematics, the online lessons for kindergarten through grade 8 [1].

A student takes the diagnostic in fall, winter and spring [8]. i-Ready builds a path of lessons from the result, and teachers can add lessons or change the order [10]. Each lesson combines instruction with practice and ends with a short, scored quiz [9]. Curriculum Associates describes the lessons as a supplement to classroom instruction [1].
credit: A nationally normed diagnostic that schools use to screen and place students [13].
Teachers stay in the loop. In the independent study, students whose teachers assigned lessons did a little better than students on the automatic path alone [2].
It has been studied from outside the company [2].

theirs: The strongest independent study we found is Darling-Aduana and Capers (2026), funded by the U.S. Institute of Education Sciences and published in the journal Online Learning [2]. It followed one southeastern district for two school years. Students who used i-Ready scored 0.04 to 0.05 standard deviations higher in math on NWEA's MAP test, which the authors put at about two weeks of growth. They call the analysis descriptive, not causal [2].

Use was low. Where i-Ready was available, 41% of students used it, and math users averaged 19.56 lessons in a school year at 24.48 minutes each: about eight hours, by our arithmetic. Students assigned many more lessons showed larger associations. The authors write that, consistent with prior research, online tools appear most effective at 40 to 100 hours a school year [2]. Across 4.3 million i-Ready students, 83% of lessons were done during school hours [4].

Curriculum Associates' headline math number, 0.24 standard deviations by grade 5, comes from a study HumRRO prepared for the company [3][8]. It applies to 676 students who met the company's usage target in all three years, compared with 665 matched students. For students with any use the estimate was 0.07 and not statistically significant [3]. Students who keep up a program for three years can differ from other students before it starts.

Evidence for ESSA rates i-Ready Personalized Instruction for math Moderate, on one quasi-experimental study published by Curriculum Associates, and does not count a company analysis limited to students who used the program with fidelity [6]. NBC News reported in 2026 that Curriculum Associates has not done a randomized controlled trial [7].
ours: The findings AMP leans on hardest: mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [11], and feedback that explains had the largest average effect across 40 studies of computer feedback [12]. The independent i-Ready study also found larger associations where students did more lessons [2]. AMP applies the first two at every problem and is built for regular use.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You run a school or district that needs a nationally normed screening test.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no test days.
You want every answer followed by the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past grade 8.
You teach a class and want to see the actual problems behind every number.

questions.question: How is AMP different from i-Ready?
questions.answer: i-Ready tests a student in fall, winter and spring and assigns lessons from the result [8][10]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does i-Ready work?
questions.answer: The strongest independent study we found reports a small positive association: users scored 0.04 to 0.05 standard deviations higher in math, at about eight hours of lessons a year, and the authors call it descriptive, not causal [2]. The company's larger number comes from students who met a usage target three years running [3].

questions.question: My child uses i-Ready at school. Can we use AMP at home?
questions.answer: Yes. AMP is a separate program. It places the learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
